source_document.body:
The Surface Transportation Board has ordered Union Pacific to turn over records concerning potential retaliation against opponents of its proposed merger with Norfolk Southern. The order follows remarks by CEO Jim Vena that customers who opposed the deal could face higher rates.
What’s Related
The board said the comments may have discouraged participation in its merger review. It warned that it “will not tolerate retaliation and will ensure that its processes are fair, transparent, and open to all stakeholders.”
Speaking at a Southwestern Association of Railroad Shippers event, Vena told attendees that Union Pacific was willing to make deals with customers. He then described what could happen if the merger did not proceed.
“If we don't do that, Union Pacific will still be there. And if I stick around, which I probably will, I'll probably increase everybody's rates that said they didn't want a seamless railroad by three or four extra percent to teach you a lesson. Thank you very much.”
Union Pacific sought to keep the remarks confidential, but the board rejected that request. It ordered the railroad to make the recording available to all parties and produce internal communications, records, and verified statements concerning potential retaliation.
RELATED: Midterm election results signal potential shifts in U.S. supply chain and freight policy
Merger opponents seek dismissal
The board also rejected Union Pacific’s request to allow private communications initiated by board members. It allowed additional parties to join the merger proceeding after the original participation deadline.
CPKC asked the board in an Oct. 30 letter to dismiss the merger application. It argued that Vena’s statements and Union Pacific’s alleged conduct had compromised the review and the board’s ability to determine whether the deal serves the public interest.
The merger applicants must respond to CPKC’s letter by Nov. 19. The board said it would address the dismissal request in a subsequent decision and consider any evidence of retaliation when deciding how the proceeding moves forward.
The Stop the Rail Merger Coalition, whose members include competing railroads, shipper organizations, and labor groups, also criticized Vena’s remarks. It argued that higher freight rates would ultimately reach consumers through higher prices for everyday goods.
Union Pacific denies retaliation
Union Pacific said it does not retaliate against customers and that their positions on the merger will not determine their rates or service. The railroad urged customers to participate in the review.
“Customers should participate freely and candidly in the Surface Transportation Board’s (STB) review,” the company said.
Union Pacific said more than 1,000 parties were participating in the proceeding, including more than 500 customers who favor the merger and account for more than 30% of its volume. It said Vena had met with hundreds of customers since the announcement.
Baird analyst Daniel Moore offered a more measured assessment in a research note issued before the board’s decision. He described Vena’s remarks as “a poor choice of words” but said they should not warrant dismissing the application.
For more details on the STB’s decision and reactions to Vena’s remarks, visit Logistics Management to read the full story.
